In answer to your question,
sir, I would say this, I should have been very glad indeed if this debate had stopped fourteen days ago. If the ministers surrounding the Prime Minister-I will leave the Prime Minister out-from the Minister of Justice down to the back bencher who is occupying the position of Minister of Agriculture, had said to the right hon. gentleman, "Your action in this matter is all wrong. There is necessity in this country with respect to unemployment; there is need to vote money for the relief of unemployment, for seed for farm relief, and we ask you to drop this resolution, which is illegal and out of order,"-if they had said this to the Prime Minister and he had come to parliament and said, "We want $50,000,000 or $100,000,000 or $150,000,000", I should have been glad to vote for it so long as the government told us what it was for. In further answer to your question, sir, may I say this. If the Prime Minister will walk in now-or, if he feels embarrassed, he can get the Minister of Justice to do it-and will drop this resolution and bring in a supply bill, or if he will get the Minister of Finance to bring in a supply bill for whatever amount may be required, we on this side of the house will gladly join with him and pass that supply bill within the next half hour.
An attempt is being made to place upon the members sitting on this side of the house the responsibility for the delay in the passing of this legislation. But that will not go down with the people of this country. We fought the constitutional question in Canada in 1926 and we are going out now and will fight it again. We who are sent here to represent the constituencies in Canada, from the Pacific to the Atlantic, are going to see that constitutional practices are observed in this country. There is no excuse for this government to say to us now that we must resurrect a dead bill, a bill which cannot be resurrected under the rules of parliament. I have no hesitation in saying that in view of the fact that this bill expired on March 1 this resolution is out of order, and consequently this discussion is also out of order, and I feel that you, Mr. Speaker, should not allow the discussion to proceed.
Why did not the government introduce this legislation in a regular manner? In the dying days of the session of 1931 the government introduced a certain resolution, not a resolution to try to revive something dead and buried, because if we can resurrect this act of 1931 we can revive it ten years hence. It makes no difference whether the act is dead one day or ten years; if it is true, as we are

told by hon. members on the other side of the house, that we can pass this legislation to revive this dead act, to give the government power whilst parliament is in session to do as they please, then in ten years' time this government, if it were in power, could come to parliament and ask to have the act revived. That, I say, is unconstitutional, and notwithstanding what has been said on the other side, we on this side of the house, standing on constitutional doctrine, will not allow such a resolution as this to go through except by closure.
What have we done? We allowed the government to put through the address in reply to the speech from the throne in a week, and for three weeks the government hesitated; it did nothing with regard to unemployment or farm relief. I do not think that this act is necessary, as I will show in a moment or two. After two years of experience the government, I submit, should have a definite policy with regard to unemployment, and I think you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that we can come to no other conclusion than that hon. gentlemen opposite have no definite policy in this matter. They are admitting that they have fallen down on the job. If, however, as I contend, they have no definite policy, and therefore wish to renew the act, then I say they should have come to parliament and introduced the same resolution they brought down a year ago. How did that resolution read? On July 24, 1931 the Prime Minister gave this notice of motion:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to confer certain powers upon the governor in council in respect to employment and farm relief; and for the maintenance of peace, order and good government in all parts of Canada; and to authorize the governor in council to expend for the said purposes out of the consolidated revenue fund such sums as may from time to time be necessary.
I respectfully submit that if the government had been seized of their proper duty with respect to unemployment, and if they felt that the proper legislation on the question was to revive the act that was passed then, instead of introducing this resolution which we are now discussing for the purpose of resurrecting a dead statute, the Prime Minister or one of his ministers should have introduced the resolution which I have just read. I say again, Mr. Speaker, that this house has no right to discuss this present resolution, and that is proved in the fact that within two days of the placing upon the order paper of the resolution now under discussion there was notice of the introduction of a bill with regard to unemployment-the strangest proce-
dure that has ever taken place in this house. The government, I presume, realized that the 1931 act was nearing its natural conclusion, and, in order to rush matters, in addition to putting upon the order paper this resolution we are now discussing they put on the order paper a bill to amend the same act-a most unusual procedure. You, Mr. Speaker, saw it yourself, because for two days, realizing the position the government had placed itself in, with your usual courtesy you did not proceed to read that bill, which should have been read every day. I say, sir, that there is no excuse for the position the house finds itself in at this moment. The government and no one else is to blame for the present impasse with regard to unemployment. It is quite possible that if the government had introduced a measure similar to the one passed in 1931 it would have been opposed on this side of the house, because there is no reason, when parliament is sitting, when the people's representatives are here to do the business of the country, why the government should introduce a bill asking for a blank cheque under which they can do whatever they deem necessary.
This government stands condemned before the people of the country so far as unemployment is concerned. Almost two years have passed since the Prime Minister and other members of his cabinet criticized the Liberal party for its attitude with regard to unemployment. Shortly after the elections a special session of parliament was called. We came down here in the month of September, 1930, and one of the first things we did was to vote a sum of $20,000,000 for the relief of unemployment. This was done with very little criticism of the government because we realized that it had not then had sufficient time to work out a policy in regard to this great question. We realized that the government had made certain promises and we wanted to give it enough rope to hang itself.
Another thing we did at that special session was to allow the government to raise the tariff. The government had two ideas in its mind, to vote money for unemployment and to raise the tariff to stop unemployment, and we agreed to both measures with very little criticism. I am sure that no hon. member within sound of my voice or no hon. member of the house can say that the opposition did anything at that time to keep the government from carrying out its policy-we gave it a free hand.
I was rather interested the other evening to hear the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. MacDonald), in his usual calm,

What did hon. members opposite proceed to do with the $20,000,000 voted for unemployment in the year 1930? Some $700,000 was spent in the province of Nova Scotia in the fall of I960. During the course of my business, and sometimes for pleasure, I drive over the roads of Nova Scotia as well as in some parts of New Brunswick. I am rather curious at times and during my drives I have noticed men employed on the roads. I would stop to talk to the different foremen, and I admit, in order to get the information I wanted, once in a while I would pretend to be something different from what I was; I even went as far as to say that once in a while I voted Tory. I found out that the men who had spent provincial money during the spring and summer of 1930 on the highways of Nova Scotia were the same men driving the same trucks and the same teams who were spending the unemployment money in the fall of 1980.

The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) endeavoured to prove the other day, in his speech, that the Prime Minister had fulfilled his pledges made during the last election. If the hon. Minister obtained for his county some favours to relieve the condition of the farmer and unemployed, since 1030, he has been shown partiality.
May I, sir, commit to Hansard a few of these pledges made by the Prime Minister and repeated in my county by the Conservative candidate and his followers. Mr. Bennett stated at Winnipeg, on June 8, 1930:
Listen you agriculturists from the west and all other parts of Canada, you have been taught to mock at tariffs and applaud free trade. Tell me, when did free trade fight for you? You say tariffs are only for manufacturers. I will make them fight for you as well. I will use them to blast a way into the markets that have been closed to you.

Then at Vancouver, June 17, 1930, he stated:
If Mr. King thinks that I will not #o build up our agricultural and industrial life that its strength will drive our products into the markets of the world, then he is wrong. For that I will do. If he thinks I will not establish new markets for those products, strive with all my heart to retain them, drive our products with all my power into new markets, into old markets, into reluctant markets, he is wrong. For that I will do.
What benefit did the farming class receive from all these pledges? Since this government has been in power, the price of farm products has decreased from 40 to SO per cent, and the farmers are experiencing a crisis unknown under the Liberal regime.
Hear, hear!

As this
question was discussed at length by my hon. friend, the member for Nicolet (Mr. Dubois), I shall not deal with it. I shall refer to the pledges made to the workmen and commit to Hansard a few of them. I shall afterward quote some figures to prove that far from decreasing the number of unemployed in my county, the government were responsible for its increase and that they even refused to help these unemployed when the money was available. As my county comprises industrial and mining centres, I Shall begin by referring to some of the promises made, during the last election, in connection with the assistance to workmen and by which he was to end unempl oyment.
The following is a statement made by the Prime Minister at Calgary, on June 12, 1930:
This is a new country and there is no excuse for unemployment in Canada if a government does its duty.
According to this statement this government is far from having done its duty. On June 17, 1930, he is quoted as saying:
Governments can regulate policies of the country so that facilities may be provided to give employment and not make it necessary for thousands to leave home and go elsewhere to get jobs to make a living.
At Sarnia, on July 16, 1930:
Someone, he said, is responsible for unemployment; not individuals but governments. Governments by their majorities in parliament are responsible for enacting all legislation.
The same day, he stated at Moncton:
Mr. King promises consideration of the problem of unemployment. I promise to end unemployment. Which plan do you like best?
I now wish, sir, to explain how he settled the unemployment question in the county of

Unemployment Continuance Act
Megantic. At Plessisville, a town of 3,000 inhabitants, on January 15, 1932, there were 230 more unemployed than on July 30, 1930.
At Black Lake, a mining centre with a population of 4,000, there were 500 to 600 people employed in July, 1930. The Conservatives had promised that if they were elected every body would have work. What happened at Black Lake? Four months after the Conservative party had assumed power, all the mines were closed, and nobody has worked in those mines since. If the government had had at heart the relief of unemployment, it would have improved the situation at Black Lake, however the contrary happened.
Under the Liberal regime I had obtained that an amount of $26,000 be included in the 1930 estimates, so as to build a post office. When the Conservatives assumed power, the plans and specifications of this building had been approved by the engineer, it was to be erected at Black Lake. Tenders had been asked and received; an order in council had been passed by this government on August 5, 1930, authorizing the construction of this post office. It was, sir, an excellent opportunity to help the unemployed. What happened? Rather than put up this post office because the money had been voted under the Liberal regime, at the request of the representative of the county, the government preferred not to carry out the construction of this post office and in that way deprived the people of work. That is the kind of help the workmen of Black Lake obtained from this government, notwithstanding all the pledges given during the 1930 election.
At Thetford mines, another mining centre with a population of 12,000, there are, to-day, 500 to 600 more people unemployed than in July, 1930. So that in Megantic county alone, this government, far from having ended unemployment as promised, has increased it by 1,200 to 1,400 men more than it was under the Liberal administration. That is how the government has settled the unemployment question.
As regards the farming class, as I stated at the outset, the price of their products has decreased 40 to 50 per cent. One thing, however, has increased in Megantic, namely taxation. The people may be deceived once but not twice. I think this is an excellent opportunity to repeat the words which the right hon. Prime Minister stated at North Vancouver, on June 18, 1930:
After I am Prime Minister on July 28, I will see that my promises are carried out or the government will go out of power trying to do so.
Well, sir, I can assure you that tire people throughout the country are waiting for that opportunity to put him out of power.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I understand correctly the effect of the motion made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) on behalf of the government this afternoon, it is to reopen a debate which had virtually drawn to a close at the time the minister spoke. The motion of the minister was that the question be now put. According to the rules of the house, the motion itself is among the number of those which are debatable, and, therefore, I conclude that all hon. members who have already spoken on the resolution before the house may speak again.
In order that there may be no mistake, I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to standing order No. 38 under the heading "Debatable Motions":
38 (1) The following motions are debatable:
Every motion,-
(a)	standing on the order of proceedings for the day (except government notices of motion for the house to go into committee at a later date);
(b)	for the concurrence in a report of a standing special committee;
(c)	for the previous question;
It is on the motion for the previous question that I am now speaking. As I have just, said, the effect of the motion of the Minister of Agriculture has been to enable every hon. member on this side of the house, or on the opposite side, who so desires, to speak again for a period of forty minutes or his allotted, time on this particular subject. I have found difficulty in understanding the reason the administration must have had for bringing forward this particular motion, and especially at this stage of the debate. As I looked through the evening papers I thought I discovered it. I may be wrong, but sometimes one gets a clue in that way. The evening papers seem to regard the motion as an application by the government of the closure rule. Evidently they are conveying to the country, no doubt from an inspired source, the information that in order to bring this debate to a close the administration has introduced closure. If I am correct in my interpretation of the rules, the effect of the motion, which the government must have brought in with full knowledge of its significance, is exactly the reverse. It has the effect of reopening the debate, and reopening it extensively.
Standing order No. 39 deals with closure. In order that there may be no mistake, and that the suggestion may not be made that

the motion introduced by the government is one of closure, I shall read the first portion of this standing order. It is as follows:
Immediately before the order of the day for resuming an adjourned debate is called, or if the house be in committee of the whole, or of supply, or of ways and means, any minister of the crown who, standing in his place, shall have given notice at a previous sitting of his intention so to do, may move that the debate shall not be further adjourned, or that the further consideration of any resolution or resolutions, clause or clauses, section or sections, preamble or preambles, title or titles, shall be the first business of the committee, and shall not further be postponed; and in either case such question shall be decided without debate or amendment; and if the same shall be resolved in the affirmative, no member shall thereafter speak more than once, or longer than twenty minutes in any such adjourned debate.
I need not read the rest of it; I believe that is sufficient. The point I wish to make clear, Mr. Speaker, to members of this house, and through the house to the country, is that the government has not introduced any motion of closure. What has been done by the motion introduced this afternoon by the Minister of Agriculture is to extend to all members of this house the privilege of speaking a second time, at a time when the debate, in regard to the first stage at least, had practically drawn to a close. As I say, what may have been the motive of the government, I leave to my hon. friends themselves to explain; and, as for the country, it may judge for itself.
This evening, I wish to deal briefly with one or two of the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture this afternoon made at the time of introducing his motion. In the first place, the minister said-I think I understood him correctly-that the reason the government had been late in bringing down this measure, which is now on the order paper and which we have been discussing for a couple of weeks, was that the former Minister of Labour, Senator Robertson, had been ill, and that, as a consequence of Senator Robertson's illness, the government had not found it possible to bring in the report of the Department of Labour with regard to the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act as early as had been hoped. It is rather extraordinary, to say the least, that we have had to wait until to-day to hear a single word of the kind expressed in the house. We have not been told before that the reason there was any delay was due to Senator Robertson's illness. This is the first intimation we have had of anything of the kind. But may I ask, Mr. Speaker, in all seriousness, whether anyone for a moment assumes that such is the reason why the government has delayed until this time to bring

in a measure which has to do with unemployment relief-the most important of all the matters 'which will have to be taken up this session?
The speech from the throne, which outlined the important business of parliament, did not contain a single word with reference to unemployment and farm relief. Surely that was not because of Senator Robertson's illness. The right hon. Prime Minister made an address of considerable length in the course of that debate. He made no reference to any policy of the government with respect to unemployment or farm relief; he made no statement with regard to any intention to bring in, at any time this session, any measure in regard to unemployment relief. Surely that was not due to Senator Robertson's illness. A little later the Minister of Labour himself (Mr. Gordon), the successor to Senator Robertson, made a speech, but it contained no reference to any policy which the government had with respect to unemployment relief. He did not say they did not have a policy because Senator Robertson had been ill; he simply made no reference to any policy.
Speakers on this side directed the attention of the house to the fact that it was a rather extraordinary thing that we had heard no statement of policy from hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to unemployment relief or with regard to the intentions of the government in that connection. I drew the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that, unemployment relief being the most important matter which this house would be called upon to consider, it was extraordinary that he had found it necessary to appoint a special committee of parliament to consider a personal matter in which he was interested, before we had any committee to discuss the question of unemployment relief or before we were told what measure of relief would be given the farmers of Saskatchewan and the other people who were suffering in the west. From this side of the house it was made clear that we were filled with amazement that the government had brought down no legislation and had indicated no policy with regard to unemployment relief in reference to Saskatchewan or any other part of Canada.
Then what happened? The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan), the former Minister of Labour, brought in an amendment on going into supply, complaining that the government had not carried out its promises with respect to unemployment relief. That amendment concluded with the statement that the government had announced no policy which was at all adequate to deal

Unemployment Continuance Act
with this particular and all-important subject. Parliament opened on Thursday, February 4, and on Tuesday, February 23, the former Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) introduced his amendment on the motion to go into supply. Was it due to Senator Robertson's illness that we had no mention of any policy, and no statement of the intentions of the government, from February 4 to February 23? Was that the reason? If it was not, why does the Minister of Agriculture with reference to the present resolution put forward a reason of that kind in the house at this stage of the debate? But what happened when the exMinister of Labour drew the attention of the house and the country to the fact that there was no statement of policy from the government, and that there was nothing anywhere on the order paper or anywhere else dealing with the subject of unemployment relief? After all this had been drawn to the attention of the government in the amendment proposed by the former Minister of Labour, on the day following, Wednesday, February 24, for the first time, there appeared in the votes and proceedings of parliament, under the name of the Prime Minister, the following notice:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.
In other words, until the government was confronted with a motion of want of confidence from this side of the house on the score that they had no policy whatever to deal with the question of unemployment, we had not so much as a sign of a resolution of any character dealing with the subject. Then we had hurriedly placed upon the order paper by the ministry a motion to extend until May 1 the present measure, or the measure that was to expire on March 1. That was all.
But how did the government proceed thereafter? Did the government the next day anxiously come to the house and say "It is getting near the end of the month and we must take up at once this resolution which appears on the order paper"? Remember, Mr. Speaker, the government has, subject to the rules of the house, the arranging of the business of the house from day to day, and the government designates the night before what particular business is to be taken up the following day. Now I want to direct your attention to the proceedings of the next few days, because I was watching, in the interests of Saskatchewan and other parts of the country, what the government were going to do in this matter of unemployment relief.
Oh, oh.
Hear, hear.

I think I shall be able to show by the records of the house, from which I am about to quote, just how carefully I was watching. On Friday, February 26, the notice appeared on the orders of the day for the first time; under government notices of motion the following resolution appeared:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.
On the same day the Prime Minister gave notice of his intention to proceed with the resolution at the next sitting. On Monday, February 29, nothing was done; that was private members' day, but I ask you now, Mr. Speaker, and those who were jeering a moment ago-including the Prime Minister himself-to look at the records of the debates in the house, as they appear in Hansard, and see what was done. I find the following at the close of the evening of Monday, February 29:
Mr. Mackenzie King: Will the Prime Minister kindly indicate the order in which government orders will be taken up to-morrow?
Mr. Bennett: Second readings first, and then supply, Departments of Agriculture and National Defence.
No word appears there with respect to this resolution concerning unemployment relief; no mention was made that the next day would be the first of March, and that chapter 58 would then expire. The Prime Minister said:
Second readings first, and then supply, Departments of Agriculture and National Defence.
Then I said:
Mr. Mackenzie King: That means the motion of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) ?
Mr. Bennett: The motion to which an amendment was moved by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River.
Mr. Mackenzie King: Is it intended to take up item 10, with respect to amending chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931?
That is, this resolution.
Mr. Bennett: I intended to take that up if we reached it, but the Senate does not meet until Wednesday. There is no point in taking it up before Tuesday.
Mr. Mackenzie King: That would be after supply, anyway?
Mr. Bennett:	Yes.
Mr. Mackenzie King:	Thank you.
I think I made it clear that evening that I was watching closely to see when the government would proceed with this measure.

The time was getting very short. If the government had intended to deal in time with unemployment under the resolution which was on the order paper, if they were genuine and bona fide in their intention, they would have proceeded immediately the opportunity was provided. What about the next day? Tuesday, March 1, was a government day, and there was no rule of the house against the measure being gone on with on that day. Moreover, the Prime Minister knew that the act would expire on March 1. If he wanted to avail himself of a technicality in order to save the situation, he could at least have made a statement the night before of his intention to deal with the matter the next day, in view of the fact that the act was expiring on the 1st of March.
But on March 1, what happened? At the very outset, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) moved the adjournment of the house to discuss seed and farm relief as matters of urgent public importance. You, Mr. Speaker, remember what happened to my hon. friend's motion. He was denied that right. He was told that he could not discuss that matter- that it was not a matter of urgent public importance at that time. Yet the act was expiring that very day, and no relief could be given thereafter until another bill went through. The hon. member rose to express that point of view but he was told by the Speaker, in the best of good faith and in accordance with what His Honour believed to be correct procedure in the house, that he could not go on. Then the debate was continued on the amendment of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, and in the course of that debate, I, myself, spoke, pointing out that on that day chapter 58 would expire. I directed the attention of parliament very pointedy to that fact.
Now, if there was great anxiety on the part of the government to deal with the question of unemployment relief under chapter 58, surely on the next day they would have made some effort to take it up without further delay. Private members' day, I hear someone say- the Prime Minister, I think. Well, at the time of adjournment on Wednesday, I called the attention of the government to the fact that the alternative for Thursday, March 3, lay between order No. 10 on the order paper, which was chapter 58, and the motion with respect to civil service salary deductions, which stood as order No. 9. I drew this to the attention of the minister who was leading the government at the time, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). As Hansard 
will show, the hon. gentleman was speaking for the government:
Mr. Stevens: We can proceed with No. 9.
Order No. 9, for Thursday, another government day, was the question of civil service salary deductions-not this resolution which is now pressed as all-impontant; not at all, but civil service salary deductions. This was extraordinary if the ministry had been intent on proceeding with chapter 58 having regard to the situation in Saskatchewan. On Thursday the question of civil service salary deductions was taken up and there was no discussion of, nor was there any mention of chapter 58. At the time of adjournment I inquired what the business for the next day would be:

Mr. Mackenzie King: What business will be taken up to-morrow?
What was the Prime Minister's reply?
Mr. Bennett: We will proceed with this debate,-
That is to say, the debate on civil service salaries.
-after which we will consider item No. 9 on the order paper.
Now, item No. 9 on the order paper of March 3 was the Heenan amendment on going into supply and not chapter 58. Did that look as though the Prime Minister was much concerned about when chapter 58 would be taken up, though we were getting further away from the date of expiry of the act? The act had expired several days before. What happened on Friday? Nothing was done with regard to chapter 58 on that day; instead, the day was taken up with the discussion of civil service salary deductions. At the adjournment I again inquired with respect to the next day's business:
Adjournment-Business of the House
Mr. Guthrie moved the adjournment of the house.
Mr. Mackenzie King: I suppose on Monday we shall have private members' resolutions?

Mr. Guthrie: In that event we will take up second reading of the bill to amend the Judges' Act, third reading of the bill to amend the Criminal Code, the bill in respect to railways- I think it is ready, and then we will go into supply.
That was for the following Tuesday. Again, nothing was said in regard to chapter 58.

That was for Monday.

Monday, yes .-I beg your pardon. That was for Monday, if we got through with private members' resolutions. That is right. But in regard to Tuesday, what happened? On Monday inquiry was again made with respect to the matter. On the order for motions on Monday afternoon, March 7, I directed the attention of the Prime Minister to the urgency of the question of unemployment and farm relief. An entire week had gone by; I had given the government, at the close of each day, an opportunity in so many ways to disclose when chapter 58, which was the measure we were concerned about, would be proceeded with. A whole week having gone by without anything having been done, in order that the government might not take a course of procedure which would be certain to precipitate a lengthy debate, and so that they might know fully in advance that we were prepared to vote any supply they wanted for relief, but that we should necessarily have to oppose, on principle, any effort that might be made to put through a bill similar to the one passed at the previous session, requiring us to give a blank cheque to the government, or requiring us to delegate to the governor in council power to legislate on peace, order and good government while parliament was in session, I drew attention to the fact that the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act had lapsed, and offered on behalf of the opposition to facilitate the passing of an interim supply bill at that time if the government would bring in a measure. Then for the first time the Prime Minister indicated that it was the intention of the government the next day to take up the resolution with respect to chapter 58.
In the meantime the government had had on the order paper notice of a bill to amend chapter 58. That notice remained on the order paper at least two or three days. You will know, Mr. Speaker, better than anyone else, the reason you did n-ot call that bill on two occasions; I think you were asked by the administration not to call it. At any rate, it stood on the order paper for some days. We on this side were asking ourselves, "What is the bill to amend chapter 58?" In all innocence, we came to the conclusion that the government, realizing that parliament would never wish to pass a bill that would give to the government power to legislate on peace, order and good government while parliament was in session, intended to wipe out that obnoxious clause and thereby seek to strengthen its position with regard to the supplying of relief under chapter 58, which
gave the governor in council a free hand to deal with the question. But to our amazement notice of this bill was subsequently dropped. What its provisions were, I do not know. Why it was not called on two or three occasions when it appeared on the order paper, though other bills were called, the Speaker and the Prime Minister I presume alone can declare. But there are the facts; the records speak for themselves.
What was the position on Monday? In order that there might be no mistake about our position and point of view as well as intention, I made the following statement, as appears at page 921 of Hansard of Monday, March 7-and this is March 22-speaking before any debate at all had commenced in relation to the question of unemployment relief :
Mr. Speaker, as we do not reach the orders of the day until late in the day, if at all to-day, there is a matter which I would like to mention to the Prime Minister on the order for motions which is of importance at the moment, and which may not have occurred to him.
There appears to be an obvious necessity for the voting of money for unemployment relief, and particularly for supplying seed grain and other forms of farm relief to those who are in need in the west. What I wish to say to my right hon. friend is that if he will bring into the house a supply bill asking for the amount that he may regard as necessary and wish to have for this month, so far as the opposition is concerned we will be prepared to do what we can to facilitate its passage rapidly through the house. We recognize that it is a week since the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act lapsed and that my right hon. friend will certainly be coming to parliament for some moneys,' for this purpose. If a supply bill is brought in at any time to provide what may be necessary for the balance of this present fiscal year, so far as the opposition is concerned we shall be prepared to agree to any suspension of the rules which will allow- the bill to go through this house with as little in the way of criticism or delay as possible.
What was the Prime Minister's reply?
Right Hon. R. B. Bennett (Prime Minister): I assure the right hon. gentleman that I appreciate his observations, but the government has not overlooked the fact that it is necessary to provide money for seed and feed. But it is not its direct responsibility; that rests with the provinces.
That was the statement made that day. The Prime Minister said further:
I thank the right hon. gentleman for his offer of assistance so far as the dealing with this emergent situation is concerned.
I then said:
I would like to make clear to my right hon. friend that one reason I mention the matter immediately is that if it is proceeded with by means of a supply bill I believe there will be no question as to the rapidity with which the bill would pass, but if my right hon. friend

lias in mind proceeding with a bill such as the one passed at last session, which was intended to meet a situation while parliament was not in session, I may say that we on this side would have to take very strong exception to proceeding in that way.
As I said, that was before any discussion had taken place on this resolution, and it was at a time when the government knew that the previous act had expired. They knew what our position was with respect to seeking to amend a statute which was dead. They knew of our willingness to give them whatever they needed in the way of supply for relief purposes. Notwithstanding that, the Prime Minister, for reasons best known to himself, proceeded to deal with this particular resolution.
That we are here, Mr. Speaker, with the Easter recess about to begin, still discussing this question, is not the fault of the opposition. It is the fault of the government in having had no policy to announce in the speech from the throne, in having had no policy announced as to the intentions towards Saskatchewan or any part of the country when the Prime Minister spoke on the address, and in having had no statement made by the Minister of Labour on the subject of unemployment relief. For more than an entire week, after notice had been given of the intention to proceed with the resolution, parliament devoted itself to other questions, notwithstanding the fact that, night after night, during the interval, the ministry was asked what business would be taken up the following day. After it had announced its intention the ministry had the freest opportunity to proceed with this measure for more than a week before the time it was proceeded with.
Under these circumstances, I do not think there can be any question as to who is responsible for the delay that has occurred up to the present time. Before I conclude my remarks this evening, I intend to indicate pretty clearly who will be responsible for any further delay. I do not think there will be much doubt as to where the opposition stands when I restate our position; indeed, there never has been. We shall soon discover what motive is underlying the tactics of the administration in this matter.
This afternoon the Minister of Agriculture gave what he termed the reason for the action of the opposition. What did he say? I confess that, if I had not heard his speech last year, I would have been amazed. However, after listening to that speech, I shall never be surprised at anything from him. In his maiden speech, the minister told the house that he

was such an innocent in the matter of politics that he did not really know the difference between a Liberal and a Conservative, that he was not interested one way or another in party politics, and he then went on to make one of the most partisan, bitterest and nastiest speeches that has ever been made by any public man in this country. What did the minister say this afternoon? He said the reason why this opposition was taking place at the present time was that the leader of the opposition was filled with revenge against Saskatchewan for having returned to this parliament himself and a few other Tories. We are discussing an unemployment relief measure which, as the Prime Minister would say, deals with the lives of men and women, with hungry and starving people, and the Minister of Agriculture talks about playing politics! I wonder what significance is to be attached to the statement that the leader of the opposition is filled with revenge against Saskatchewan? If that is not playing politics, the most diabolical politics which can be conceived of, I should like to know what is. What revenge would I have against Saskatchewan? Was not Saskatchewan the province which gave such splendid support to the Liberal party as to ensure its continuance in office from 1925 to 1930? Am I unmindful of the fact that I stand to-night in this house honoured with the representation of a constituency in the province of Saskatchewan, and that, taking byelections into account, Prince Albert in Saskatchewan has on four different occasions returned me to this parliament? I speak as a representative of the province of Saskatchewan, and I intend to speak more particularly from that point of view during the concluding part of my remarks.
I challenge the Minister of Agriculture to point in the course of my entire public career to one single act of mine which has been inspired by the spirit of revenge. Only those who are themselves capable of that kind of thing would think of imputing that sort of action to others. As for the remarks of the minister, I am prepared to treat them as being beneath contempt. When the people of Saskatchewan read what the minister said in this house this afternoon in regard to this measure, when they learn what he has had to offer as a reason for not giving them relief and giving them the seed and feed that they need, their appreciation of the minister, if it ever amounted to anything, will cease to be of much account.
Why has the opposition taken the course it has with regard to the resolution before us? We took this course for one reason, and one

Unemployment Continuance Act
reason only. It was a very simple reason but a very powerful one-it was the right course to take, that is all. It was not from any political motive, it was not from any desire-
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen opposite cannot understand that. They are so accustomed to every move being actuated by some political partisan motive that they are unable to appreciate a contrary course though it be the obvious truth. What are the rules of this house governing supply? One has only to look at the rules to discover how the administration is supposed to go about getting supply for any purpose. Did we say: "If you bring in supply for unemployment relief we will oppose it"? Did we say: "If you make your measure broad we will oppose it; if you make your measure narrow we will oppose it; if you make it this way or that way we will oppose it"? Had we done that, there would have been some ground for saying that we had offered opposition. But we did the very reverse; we left it to hon. gentlemen opposite to make whatever motion they liked, so long as it was in accordance with the rules and procedure of this parliament, the rules and procedure which govern not only the parliament of Canada, but the parliament of every self-governing country under the British flag. We have endeavoured, as representatives of the people, to secure to them their rights and liberties, and preserve so far as we are able to, the control of taxation, a very important matter in times like this. We said: It is our duty, if we have any duty at all, to see that the government acts in accordance with the rules and procedure which are the known practices, traditions and customs of the House of Commons and of parliament. That is all we sought, that is all we ever asked. But we have at this time emphasized the reason for so doing.
We have pointed out that whatever the government may have done under pressure pressure upon themselves, pressure which they have exerted upon us, pressure for any reason that you like, leaving aside altogether the motive-whatever they may have done for those reasons and whatever, under pressure, may have gone through the house in the form of a statute giving them power, while parliament was not in session, to deal, without reference to parliament, with matters which should be the subject of legislation by parliament only, we could not undertake to give them those powers while parliament itself was in session. That has been the point, and that
is the whole point to-day. Whatever, for any reason, may have been necessary to deal with an emergency when parliament was not in session, whatever may have been necessary to deal with an Unknown condition when parliament might not be in session, cannot possibly apply when the king's representative in this country is surrounded, not only by his ministers but by the members of parliament whom he has summoned from all parts of Canada to deal with great questions of this kind. That is the position.
How can it be contended that it is not making a mockery of parliament for His Majesty's representative to cause to assemble members from all parts of the country to deal with a great question, only to have them told that they are to be deprived of their rights of dealing with such matters; that they must delegate those rights to the ministry of the day, in order to permit the ministry to enact by order in council whatever they wish? The Prime Minister says: in consideration of all this, we, the ministry, will reward you. the representatives of the people, by presenting you on the day following with copies of the orders in council which we have passed. I ask: Could a greater indignity to a parliament be conceived of than an action of the kind?
It is for reasons like this and for that alone, we have taken the position we have. AVe shall continue, and we must continue to take it, unless we are going to abandon for all time in this country, the authority, the supremacy, the rights of parliament and all that is associated therewith. AVhy have a parliament at all, if the executive alone is to deal in secret council with all such questions, pass laws, fix fines, establish penalties, award contracts running into a million dollars at a time, without any reference to the people's representatives who are assembled in this house? Does the government think, that, because there are men and women anxious for food, clothing and work, they are going to be so blind politically they will not recognize that there is a responsibility upon parliament to proceed in the right way to do the right thing? Nobody is asking the ministry to do the wrong thing. A\7e all agree that relief should be given. AVe all agree that, whatever amount the ministry says they need, we will give them, if only they ask for it in the right way.
What is left then? One of two motives alone can account for the attitude of the ministry. One is that the ministry must intend to do something which will not bear the light of day. There must be something they are determined to do which would not be

The only other motive can be that the Prime Minister of the day has said: I am going to take a certain course, and I shall not change from it whether it be right or wrong; I am going to be a dictator; I am going to do as I please with parliament, and this might as well be conceded first as last. That is the only reason parliament is being forced to proceed in this way. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada are not prepared, as has been said time and again here, to trust any government with powers of dictatorship as long as we have a constitutional parliament assembled in this country. Least of all will they be prepared to trust my right hon. friend with any such powers. He has been in office now long enough, not only for the House of Commons, but for the country to know what his tendencies, bis methods, his principles are in the matter of government. And I say, if for no other reason than, as shown here the other evening in the most conclusive language, because of the stand which he himself has taken in dealing with the House of Commons in many matters, this house will never surrender to him rights which have been won for the people through their representatives.
May I point out something else? I said that we were taking the course we were because it was the right course. As is well known, if you start on a right course and follow it, you never have to change. It is equally true, if you start on a wrong course and keep following it, you do not know where it is going to lead. It is certainly not going to lead to anything better; it is bound to lead steadily to something worse. At the outset, in regard to this measure, we pointed out to the ministry that, by taking a wrong course they would get into deeper and deeper water all the time. We wish to avoid :hat.
I should like to point out why the ministry, even now, should correct its course as speedily as possible. Assuming the motion brought forward this afternoon had not been moved, and this debate had terminated this evening, as would probably have been the case, with a decision that we would go into committee on the resolution. What would then have been the next step? We would have gone into committee on the resolution. What is the first question that would have come up? Assume that is the stage we had now reached. The chairman of committees would read the resolution, and, as leader of the opposition, I would be obliged to ask whether

it was within the competence of parliament to entertain a resolution of the kind. To what does the resolution relate? It relates to a dead act. It reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.
Chapter 58 of the statutes of 1931 expired on March 1. This is March 22, so that the statute has been a dead letter for three weeks. It is a dead statute. Is parliament to be subjected to the further indignity of having to consider something that is dead, to amend something that has no life, something that no longer exists? The Prime Minister the other day, when we were discussing the salaries of civil servants, gave parliament the assurance that this cut in the salaries would end on March 31 of next year; that the act would expire at that time. What did he say about the expiry, so that all would be doubly sure, the civil servants after March 31, 1933, need have no fear about that act ever troubling them again? I have under my hand my right hon. friend's words as they appear on page 564 of Hansard of February 26. He said:
As the resolution itself indicates, the bill will expire on the 31st day of March, 1933. It has no vigour or life beyond that date.
He says that act will expire on March 31, 1933. The act it is proposed to amend says in its context that it will expire on March 1 of this year. If the Prime Minister's words are to apply in one case as in the other- and I do not think anyone can dispute that they are equally applicable-then this statute which expired on March 1 has had no vigour or life beyond that date. Are we, the people's representatives here assembled, to be asked to consider this dead thing, and to spend our time, in the name of affording unemployment relief, in seeing what we can do about amending something that doesn't exist?
Assume that it is ruled, dead or not, we must consider it. What is the next step? The Prime Minister comes forward with a motion to amend this wretched resolution that relates to this dead object. What happens then? Immediately the committee is confronted with the rules on which the chairman of committees will have to base a decision. He is faced with this: It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which it is proposed. This amendment is relevant to what? to a dead thing. Is the chairman of committees to place on record, for the guidance of subsequent parliaments, a decision that, simply because

one ministry has started on a wrong course, hereafter any government may amend a statute that has ceased to exist, and that it shall be the serious business of parliament to consider matters of the kind? I say that it is that kind of thing which we wanted to spare the ministry, which we wanted to spare the Commons, which we wanted to spare the country. I say that, if this resolution passes, that will have to be the first question which will have to be raised, and I submit in all seriousness again, Mr. . Speaker, that, in the interests of this parliament, and of the parliamentary institutions and rules and practices of this house which we value so highly, great care should be taken not to run the risk of having decisions given for any immediate purpose which may be of embarrassment to all parliaments of Canada for all time to come.
But more than that. Suppose the chairman of the committee rules that it is in order to amend this dead statute, and the amendment would be that we revive this dead thing, that parliament resurrect statute 58 and give it life. Parliament can do that, not by amending a statute that does not exist, but by introducing a new bill. The ministry can bring in a bill to-morrow saying, "By this measure the provisions of what was chapter 58 1931 are hereby re-enacted." That in all probability would be the equivalent of the terms of the new statute. That is a perfectly proper way to proceed. If they were determined to deal with the matter by chapter 58, that is the way the ministry should have proceeded, instead of proceeding by way of a resolution that seeks to amend something that has long ceased to exist and has gone into oblivion.
But supposing it has been ruled that the amendment is in order, and assume that after discussing it the amendment carries and the amended resolution carries. What question is raised then? Immediately you are face to face with other rules of this house, rules, again, which have been enacted by the wisdom of preceding parliaments to safeguard the public treasury, because all parliaments in past generations have felt that the most sacred of all their duties was the safeguarding of the public treasury. It is for that reason that the measures by which a ministry draws money from the public treasury are surrounded with more in the way of caution and safeguards than any other class of measures that can be conceived of and which may be brought into a. deliberative assembly.
What are the rules of the house in regard to measures which purport to draw money from the treasury? They must, first of all,
receive the approval of His Excellency the Governor General. We sometimes smile when we hear hon. gentlemen opposite repeat in parrotlike fashion that His Excellency the Governor General has been apprised of the subject matter of the resolution and commends it to the favourable consideration of the house. A great many think that is a mere form of words, but I hope I may assume that my right hon. friend has taken the same course as I did when Prime Minister, which was to obtain from His Excellency the Governor General a standing permission to make that announcement to the house in his name upon one consideration, that I, as Prime Minister, would take care to see that, if there was the slightest doubt about any resolution not being entirely in accordance with the general rules and practices of the house, such a resolution would be presented to him in advance so that His Excellency might have the opportunity to pass upon it. That is the only course a constitutional Prime Minister can take. The Crown, Mr. Speaker, still has some responsibility. It might not seem so in view of some of the things that have already happened in this session of parliament. It might seem that the Crown does not count, for anything, except to be swept to one side, but the Crown does count for something even in the affairs of this parliament of Canada; and the rule applies here.
Xow may I draw your attention to this, Mr. Speaker? The first question that must be asked of the ministry when they have chapter 58 in resurrected form before the committee for consideration is this: Has the consent of His Excellency the Governor General been obtained? We all know that His Excellency's consent has not yet been obtained. I put that question now to the ministry: Have you obtained the consent of His Excellency the Governor General to whatever bill is going to be brought in here later, following this resolution? You know you have not. It is not sufficient to say that His Excellency the Governor General gave his consent to the resolution now on the order paper in the month of February when statute 58 was still alive. Certainly His Excellency may be assumed to have given consent to the introduction of a resolution which related to chapter 58 while chapter 58 was still in existence, because His Excellency would then be -consenting to a course with respect to something that was vital, something that had a future. Had the proper course been followed, and that resolution been gone on with before the statute expired, certainly His

But I submit that all that can be said with respect to His Excellency's consent is that it is applicable, unless expressly provided otherwise, to moneys that may be paid out after the bill relating thereto has received royal assent; it does not, except with expressed provision, apply to retroactive payments. A resurrected measure of the kind being thought of before becoming law would have to pass the Commons and the Senate and receive the assent of His Excellency. Until His Excellency's assent-not consent-has been given, expenditure of moneys under that act could not be made. When assent is given, it is for expenditures of money to be made under its provisions from the time it is passed; it is not an assent to retroactive payments unless consent to a resolution expressly mentioning retroactive payments has been given before the bill itself was introduced. The ministry cannot so construe it. They cannot put the crown in the embarrassing position of being a party to voting the moneys of the people for the purpose of meeting payments that have become due before the measure itself under which they are to be made is law. There must be some special authority in advance so to do. So I say to the ministry, even now, before you begin to bring the Crown into this position of embarrassment-the Prime Minister laughs. That appears to be the Prime Minister's chief role in this parliament, to laugh, to laugh.

I say again,
Mr. Speaker, that the people of this country, and particularly the people of Saskatchewan, have a right to know the situation before they are again hoaxed in a matter of this kind by the present administration.
If a bill is to be passed, and something will have to be passed to make good payments which have been made or may have become

due since the first of March and up to now for unemployment and farm relief. There is existing at present no legal authority for any such payments; everything done in that matter since the first of March, if anything has been done, is illegal. The only way whatever has been done can be legalized is by this parliament at some stage legalizing it-in that event, a bill will have to be brought in sufficiently broad to legalize what has already been done illegally, and a bill to that effect will have to be preceded by a resolution which will have received de novo the consent of His Excellency the Governor General. The process will have to be started all over again from the very beginning before payments can be made in respect to all obligations undertaken in regard to farm and unemployment, relief between March 1 up to the present time. So I say that if we have been contending, as we have, for the right course to be pursued, it has been, amongst other things, to avoid all these pitfalls, to preserve the practices and the traditions of parliament, and to see that matters were expedited in the right way.
Let me say this: The ministry itself is not in ignorance of the correct way to go about obtaining money from parliament. During the course of this very debate, our proceedings were halted one day to receive a message from His Excellency the Governor General signed by his own hand, and there was presented to this House of Commons by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) further supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1932, totalling $1,059,474.33, and there was another supplementary estimate for 1931-1932 in regard to the Canadian National Steamships. Why was there no supplementary estimate, I ask, for seed and feed relief for Saskatchewan? Was that not needed just as much as any of the things mentioned in the particular estimates which were brought down the other day? Let me mention a few of the items in those estimates. Here is an item for External Affairs, Paris; something for Geneva; here is something for the Montreal harbour commission; here is something with regard to governor general's warrants; here is something for public printing and stationery; something for contingencies, expenses of committees and clerical assistance in the House of Commons; here is something for the Yukon territory. Is this question of unemployment and farm relief not as important as any of the matters mentioned in these supplementary estimates? Why, them, did not the ministry include in these supplementary estimates an estimate for the relief of distress in Saskatchewan? They

know as well as we do that an estimate of that kind might have been included in a single line on this sheet. All hon. members on this side of the house would have agreed to pass it, and it would have been thoroughly in order and regular. Therefore, hon. gentlemen opposite cannot say we have been blocking them in any matter of mere procedure. If they had taken the same procedure in regard to the relief of the unemployed and the relief of distress in Saskatchewan, as they have adopted in connection with matters of very secondary importance, they would have long ago brought in a supply bill and already had the moneys required.
Now .may I add these fui'ther remarks: I do not think the followers of the right hon. gentleman opposite have even yet a correct idea of what the ministry has in mind, or what its intentions may be. Last week, during the course of this debate, we listened to the remarks of the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. MacDonald). What did he say? He said that the government is simply asking parliament for an extension of two months to carry out commitments already made. Throughout the country, the press has been repeating that statement; it has been saying that all the government is asking is to make good the commitments they have already made. I made it very clear that if such were the case we would end our oppostion at once. When the hon. member for Cape Breton was speaking I asked him, as recorded at page 1206 of Hansard, the following question:
Does he say that the bill to be introduced goes only to the length of asking that the government shall have authority to complete the commitments already made?
In reply to that the hon. member said:
That is the intention and justification for this resolution.
Then I made the further statement:
May I tell him that if the Prime Minister is prepared to introduce a hill based on the hon. member's interpretation given a moment ago, that is, a bill containing power only to meet the commitments that already have been made, we on this side will stop our opposition at once.
That was an assurance from this side of the house that, if all the government was seeking was to make good in the next two months commitments already made, we would stop our opposition at once. I say the mere fact that an hon. member of this house, a supporter of the administration, made the statement to which I have referred, and made it seriously, shows that hon. gentlemen opposite
do not understand even yet the intentions of the government.
May I outline the present position. So that there may be no mistake, let me repeat what I said before the debate commenced, and what hon. members on this side of the house have said over and over again. At the same time let it be remembered, we are on the eve of an Easter recess. Tomorrow evening at six o'clock parliament will adjourn until the following Tuesday. I desire to make it perfectly clear that, between now and that time, if the government wishes to proceed with regard to unemployment relief as they have proceeded with these other matters which they brought in in the supplementary estimates, we will do all in our power to see that the rules of this house are suspended to permit a supply bill being put through tomorrow afternoon and the necessary supply for relief voted before adjournment at six o'clock. I want the people of Saskatchewan to know tomorrow night, beyond all possibility of mistake, if they have to go through this Easter period without relief, who is responsible for the fact. They will know where the responsibility lies if the course I have suggested is not taken. I am making my speech this evening in order that the ministry, which has the forenoon to arrange such matters, may present an estimate and draft a supply bill in the same form as they have always done on other occasions. If they will do that, we will do all in our power to expedite its passage through all its stages.
We rwill go a step farther. There is on the order paper at the moment a motion to go into committee of supply, and an amendment thereto standing in the name of Mr. Heenan. Until that motion is disposed of, the house cannot go into committee of supply. If the government will bring down a supply bill, stating their requirements for purposes of relief, we will be prepared to vote on Mr. Heenan's amendment at once, and get rid of it so that it will be out of the way, in order that the house may immediately go into committee to consider the necessary supply for unemployed and farm relief. We would not press the debate on the Heenan amendment any further; we are perfectly willing to get it out of the way, provided that is in order to have the decks perfectly clear to proceed in supply with unemployment relief. There can be no mistake about our position in this respect.

Any legislation based upon the measure the government are now asking us to consider cannot extend beyond the first of May. But the Premier of Saskatchewan states that that province must have assistance until another crop is assured, in other words, until, say, the 1st of September. Supposing we were to consent to the passage of the proposed measure, would it meet the situation in Saskatchewan? Certainly not, according to the statement of the premier of that province. He says the farmers of Saskatchewan will have to have sufficient supply voted to help them until they are assured of their crop.
Speaking to the people of Saskatchewan, as a representative of the province of Saskatchewan, as well as leader of my party, may I say what the Liberal party in Canada is prepared to do for that province. If to-morrow, Wednesday, before this house adjourns, the Prime Minister, or any member of his government, brings in a bill stating how much money the government requires in the way of supply, to care for the unemployed and for the relief of distress in Saskatchewan-in fact, for relief in all parts of Canada-not merely until the first of May, but until the first of September, we will, so far as it lies within our power so to do, put that bill through the house before Easter adjournment.
We will go even a step farther, so that there may be no mistake about our position. The Imperial conference is to be held next summer; quite certainly the government will want time to consider matters in connection with it. Once the Easter recess is over, there will be great anxiety to deal with fiscal problems and to get away from those which have to do with unemployment and relief. If to-morrow, 
the government will say how much they need by -way of unemployment and farm relief funds, not merely until the first of May, not merely until the first of September, but until March 31, 1933, and on their responsibility as a ministry will state the amount, I say that all hon. members in this Liberal opposition will do their utmost to see that the necessary supply required is voted to-morrow.
